subtitle: The Science of History · Civilization · Statehood · Independence

chapters.title: History as a Science: Subject, Sources and Methods

blocks.narration: Welcome to the complete video guide to the History of Uzbekistan, weeks one to four. In the next half hour we travel from the first rock carvings of the Palaeolithic to the proclamation of independence in nineteen ninety-one. You will learn what history is as a science, how Central Asia became a center of world civilization, how three thousand years of statehood produced the republics of nineteen twenty-four, and how Uzbekistan won and built its independence. Every date, name and number comes directly from the course guide.

blocks.title: History as a Science
blocks.subtitle: What is history, and how do we know the past?
blocks.narration: Chapter one. Before we can study the history of Uzbekistan, we must understand history itself: what it is as a science, what counts as evidence, and how historians check the truth. This chapter gives you the concepts, the sources and the methods that we will use in every later chapter.

blocks.heading: What Is History?
bullets: the life of society in the past
re-thinking the past: what, when, how
cause and effect between past and present
blocks.narration: History is the study of the life of society in the past, in connection with the present and the expectations of the future. Its raw material is evidence, the fact: an inquiry into the past on the basis of evidence, an attempt to re-think what happened, when and how. Nehru called it the story of man's struggle through the ages. Alisher Navoi added that history records which ruler was cruel and who held the banner of justice, and Fitrat defined it as the subject that studies the causes of the prosperity and the crisis of our people in the past.

blocks.heading: The Nature of History
bullets: man in time — every event has its moment
a dialogue between past and future
blocks.narration: The lecture gives eleven propositions; four matter most. First, history is the science of man, the story of man's struggle through the ages. Second, man in time: every event takes place at a definite moment, and time gives perspective. Third, man in space: politics, society, economy and culture grow out of the geographical context. Fourth, history is a dialogue between the events of the past and the gradually emerging ends of the future. And history is not only narration but analysis: causal connections are uncovered and compared with other societies. Continuity and coherence are its necessary conditions.

blocks.heading: Fact, Thought and Experience
bullets: thought — a viewpoint formed from facts
the order: experience, thought, then fact
blocks.narration: Three key points unlock the essence of history. Experience is a combination of positive and negative notions about man or the historical process, their analysis and interpretation. Thought is an idea or a point of view formed out of many facts. Fact is the raw material of history: the study of what happened, when and how. The most important conclusion of the lecture: experience comes first, then thought, and only then fact. Knowing many facts by itself does not mean knowing history. Without facts history turns into literature, but facts are merely instruments leading to reality.

blocks.heading: Doing History: The Case at the Qadi's Court
blocks.problem: One source distorts; several sources create an objective picture.

steps.text: A petitioner complains to the qadi against his brother
The brother refuses to divide the paternal land
From the first document alone, he looks like a bad man
A second document: he had offered half the land's value
The income of the land fed only one family
Compare sources — one distorts, several give the truth

blocks.narration: Here is a real case from the lecture. In the Samarkand archive there is a document of a petitioner to the qadi, the judge in a Muslim court, against a brother who would not divide the paternal land. From this one document you might call the brother a bad man. But a second document shows that the brother had offered his sibling half the value of the land, so that he could buy land elsewhere or take up trade. Why? Because the income from the land was sufficient for only one family. The lesson is the golden rule of source work: one source distorts, several sources create an objective picture. Always compare before you judge.

blocks.heading: Primary and Secondary Sources
blocks.narration: Historians divide sources into two great families. A primary source was created by a witness or a participant of an event, during the period under study: manuscripts and archival materials, government documents, maps, objects and artifacts, oral history, the contemporary press. A secondary source was created considerably later, or by a person who took no part in the events: books and articles that analyze the question, usually with bibliographies leading to other sources. The rules are simpler for secondary sources: they are always after the event, and they describe primary sources without reproducing them verbatim.

blocks.heading: The Historian's Toolkit
blocks.narration: History includes a family of auxiliary disciplines. Archaeology is the scientific study of the material remains of past human life, from stone tools to palaces; over one hundred and fifty years of excavations have revealed the region's way of life. Ethnography describes the ordinary social behaviors of a group of people, using participant observation. Numismatics is the scientific analysis of money: through coins it studies rulers, culture, religion and metallurgy. Chronology arranges events in time and synchronizes the reigns of rulers. Source studies follows the rule trust but verify. Historiography studies the methods of historians themselves.

blocks.heading: Who Writes History? The Case of Amir Timur
blocks.problem: Why can one and the same figure be assessed differently?

steps.text: History is written by the victors
Governments and funds pay for its writing
Under Soviet rule, Timur was studied negatively
In independence years: raised to national hero
Research showed: trade, architecture, science

blocks.result: The assessment depends on the interpreter
blocks.narration: History is written by the victors. Governments and funds pay for the writing of history and want to read it the way they imagine it, so historians have often depended on rulers. That is why we must compare data from different sources. The lecture's example is Amir Timur. Under Soviet rule he was studied mostly negatively, under the influence of ideology. In the years of independence his status was raised to that of a national hero, because research showed that he developed trade, architecture, international relations and science. The same holds for Genghis Khan: for the Mongols he is a hero. The conclusion: the assessment of a historical figure depends on the position of the interpreter.

items: History — inquiry into the past on evidence
Experience first, then thought, then fact
blocks.narration: Let us fix chapter one. History is an inquiry into the past on the basis of evidence. Of the three key points, experience matters most, then thought, then fact. Primary sources come from eyewitnesses; secondary sources analyze them later. One source distorts, several create an objective picture. And the assessment of a figure depends on the position of the interpreter.

chapters.title: Central Asian Civilization: From Petroglyphs to Proto-Cities

blocks.title: Central Asian Civilization
blocks.subtitle: From the first rock carvings to proto-cities
blocks.narration: Chapter two. Here we prove that Turan, or Turkestan, is an integral part of world civilization: settled life, cities, art and irrigation arose here independently. We follow the region from the petroglyphs of the Old Stone Age to the proto-cities of the Bronze Age.

blocks.heading: Civilization and Central Asia
bullets: one of the centers of world civilization
blocks.narration: Civilization is a complex human society, usually made up of cities, from the Latin civitas, with developed government, culture and industry. The best-known world civilizations are the Egyptian, Babylonian, Chinese, Indian, Greco-Roman and Arab. The concept of Central Asia was introduced by Alexander von Humboldt in the nineteenth century: a vast territory, also called Turkestan, from Uyghuria to the Caspian, from the south of Siberia to Iran, the same space as Turan, called Middle Asia and Kazakhstan in Soviet times. And the newest research has proved that this region is one of the centers of world civilization.

blocks.heading: The Long Road to Settled Life
blocks.narration: The occupation of the region began as early as the Lower Palaeolithic: our sources are petroglyphs, rock drawings and stone tools. In the Mesolithic an important technological achievement appeared, the bow and arrows. Then came the Neolithic Revolution of the sixth and fifth millennia before Christ: the transition to a producing economy, almost simultaneously with Western Asia. Jeitun was settled from about seven thousand two hundred to four thousand five hundred before Christ, and agriculture developed there for the first time in the region. From five thousand five hundred to three thousand five hundred before Christ, the Kelteminar fishers lived in the deltas. Finally, the Bronze Age brought metallurgy and the first proto-cities.

blocks.heading: Jeitun, Kelteminar, Hissar
blocks.narration: Three Neolithic cultures are key here. Jeitun, in southern Turkmenistan, was settled from seven thousand two hundred to four thousand five hundred before Christ, in the Kopet Dag foothills; sheep and goats were domesticated, and the region's first agriculture developed here. Kelteminar is a culture of settled fishers of the Karakum and Kyzylkum, in the deltas of the Amu Darya and the Zeravshan, from five thousand five hundred to three thousand five hundred before Christ; its huge houses, twenty-four by seventeen meters, housed a clan of one hundred to one hundred twenty. The Hissar culture, seven thousand to two thousand before Christ, developed in the Kafirnigan and Vakhsh valleys.

blocks.heading: The Bronze Age
blocks.narration: The Bronze Age introduced metallurgy: stone tools began to be replaced by metal ones. Irrigation, artificial watering, and urban planning appeared in the economy, alongside the alloying of metals and proto-urban settlements; large centers of more than ten hectares arose, such as Kara-depe and Namazga-depe. The sites include Altyn-depe, Jarkutan, Namazga-depe, Zamanbaba in the Bukhara area and Sapalli, proto-urban settlements. The economy rested on two pillars, agriculture and cattle breeding. In art, the unified culture split into a western and an eastern variant: the west is multicoloured painted ware with geometric ornament, while in the east the ornaments are simpler, straight parallel lines along the rims.

blocks.heading: Neolithic versus Bronze Age
blocks.narration: How do you tell the Neolithic from the Bronze Age on an exam? The Neolithic, in the sixth and fifth millennia before Christ, means the Neolithic Revolution: settled life, agriculture, cattle breeding and fishing, the building of houses, early crafts, and pottery without a potter's wheel. The Bronze Age means metallurgy: stone tools are replaced by metal ones, artificial irrigation appears, together with urban planning and proto-cities, and the settlements grow more complex. The key marker of the boundary is the appearance of metal and of cities. Art also split into two schools of painted pottery, the western and the eastern.

blocks.heading: Migrations and Tolerance
blocks.narration: The lecture singles out the great waves of migration to Central Asia. The Indo-European peoples came first, the Iranians and the Indians. Then came the migrations of the Jews; of the Turks, whose penetration is dated to the fourth to sixth centuries; of the Arabs, who came in the seventh and eighth centuries, the Arab conquests beginning in seven hundred four; and of the Mongols in the thirteenth century. The mixing of the local inhabitants with newcomers of different ethnic groups led to the formation of diasporas and of tolerance towards different groups, inside and outside the country.

blocks.heading: Jeitun or Kelteminar?
blocks.problem: Where did agriculture first develop in Central Asia, and why there?

steps.text: Jeitun: southern Turkmenistan, Kopet Dag foothills
Settled 7200–4500 BC, short interruptions
Sheep and goats domesticated; hunting added
Kelteminar: deltas, settled fishers
Agriculture first developed at Jeitun

blocks.narration: A classic exam question: find the place where agriculture first developed in Central Asia. Jeitun lies in southern Turkmenistan, in the foothills of the Kopet Dag, and was settled approximately from seven thousand two hundred to four thousand five hundred before Christ, with possible short interruptions. Sheep and goats had been domesticated there, but the inhabitants supplemented their diet by hunting. Here, for the first time in the region, agriculture developed. Kelteminar is the culture of settled fishers of the Karakum and the Kyzylkum, in the deltas of the Amu Darya and the Zeravshan; its people lived in huge communal houses and did not take up farming. So the answer is Jeitun.

Chapter two in brief. Civilization is a society of cities, from the Latin civitas. Central Asia is Humboldt's term for the historical Turkestan, or Turan. In the Neolithic, remember Jeitun with the first agriculture, Kelteminar the fishers, and the Hissar culture. The Bronze Age brought metal, irrigation and proto-cities. And the waves of migration, Iranians, Indians, Jews, Turks, Arabs, Mongols, formed diasporas and taught the region tolerance.

chapters.title: Three Thousand Years of Statehood: From Bactria to the Timurids

blocks.title: Three Thousand Years of Statehood
blocks.subtitle: From the first proto-states to Amir Timur
blocks.narration: Chapter three, the heart of the course: about three thousand years of statehood. We move from the first proto-states of Northern Bactria through the Samanids and their diwans to Amir Timur, and on to the three khanates. Forms of states, titles of rulers, systems of government, the most fact-saturated block of the guide.

blocks.heading: What Is Statehood?
bullets: peoples and tribes unified by law
blocks.narration: Statehood is the formation of political entities: the transformation of adats and tribal-clan forms, with their limited regulation, into definite legal structures under a specific ruler and system. Statehood on the territory of Uzbekistan developed for about three thousand years; the first sprouts appeared in Khorezm, after urban construction grew. The form of statehood was mostly a monarchy until nineteen twenty, and that is why it is studied in the chronological order of dynasties. In the world, the emergence of statehood goes back to the Chalcolithic, in Egypt and Mesopotamia, in the fourth and third millennia before Christ.

blocks.heading: The Six Periods of Ancient Statehood
blocks.narration: First: early state forms in Northern Bactria, in the second half of the second millennium before Christ. Second: from the beginning of the first millennium to the end of the sixth century before Christ, the formation of the states of Bactria, Sogd and Khorezm. Third: from the early fifth century to three hundred twenty-nine before Christ, the control of the Achaemenids. Fourth: from the end of the fourth to the end of the second century before Christ, the Hellenistic states, Khorezm and Kangju. Fifth: from the end of the second century before Christ to the first century of our era, the Kushan kingdom. Sixth: the first to third centuries, the final stage of ancient statehood.

blocks.heading: The Primary States
blocks.narration: Four primary states must be known. Bactria covered present-day Afghanistan, the south of Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, with the capital Bactra; in the sixth century it was occupied by the Achaemenids, then by Alexander the Great. Sogd was central Uzbekistan, capital present-day Samarkand; an Achaemenid satrapy, it was attacked by Alexander in three hundred twenty-nine before Christ and conquered two years later. Khorezm was not attacked by Alexander: its ruler was wise in foreign policy, and it preserved its independence until the Arab conquest. Dayuan was the state of the Fergana Valley; Zhang Qian noted seventy large and small cities there.

blocks.heading: Forms of States and Titles of Rulers
blocks.narration: States are classified in two ways. By genetic structure: autochthonous states, created by the indigenous population, such as Kangju and Khorezm; and externally created states, built by conquerors, such as the Achaemenid Empire and Greco-Bactria. By typology of rule: a kingdom as an absolute monarchy, like the Achaemenids and Greco-Bactria; a theocratic monarchy with religious legitimisation, the Kushan kingdom; a confederative kingdom with a limited monarchy, Kangju, with the Great Yuezhi; and a domain, the hereditary power of tribal leaders. Now the titles: Bago pauro, Son of God, in Bactria; the Iranian shahanshah, king of kings; the Turkic yabgu; and amir, sultan, khan and emperor.

blocks.heading: The Samanids: Dargah and Ten Diwans
blocks.narration: Now the governance of the Samanids, important for tests. The head of state was the emir; the provinces were governed by his governors. Together with the royal court, the dargah, legislation and the judiciary, ten centralized military-civilian departments, the diwans, operated. The main one was the diwan of the vizier, controlling all administrative, political and economic institutions. Then: the mustawfi, finances; amid al-mulk, diplomacy and state papers; sahib ash-shurta, the guard and military affairs; sahib al-barid, the post and secret surveillance of rulers; the muhtasib, markets, measures and weights; the mushrif, revenues and expenditures; plus the diwans of judicial affairs, state lands and waqf, charitable lands.

blocks.heading: Timur and the Timurids
blocks.narration: Timur besieged Balkh: the fortifications were breached, Amir Husayn was defeated, and on the tenth of April, thirteen seventy, Timur came to power. He proclaimed the Chinggisids Suyurgatmish and Sultan Mahmud titular khans, an example of a limited monarchy, of the monarch as a symbol of the unity of the nation. His army occupied ten million square kilometers, from Eastern Turkestan to the Mediterranean, from Siberia to the Indian Ocean. The last design, the campaign against China, was interrupted by his death in fourteen hundred and five, at seventy. The Timurid dynasty ruled until fifteen hundred and seven; its Renaissance gave us Ulugbek, Navoi and Babur.

blocks.heading: From the Timurids to the Three Khanates

events.text: Timur dies at 70; China campaign off

blocks.narration: After Timur came the division into small states. The Shaybanids ruled first, then the Ashtarkhanids; the monarchical form of statehood survived until nineteen twenty. In the end the region was divided into three states: the Bukhara Emirate, the Khanate of Khiva and the Khanate of Kokand. It was precisely these three states that were conquered by the Russian Empire in the second half of the nineteenth century. On the screen you see the anchor dates: thirteen seventy, fourteen five, fifteen seven, then the Shaybanids and Ashtarkhanids, the Russian conquest, and nineteen twenty, when the Soviet period begins. Remember the sequence for the exam.

blocks.heading: Why Did Timur Appoint Titular Khans?
blocks.problem: Timur held real power — why did he proclaim others as khans?

steps.text: The title of khan came with the Turks
Legitimacy: lineage traced to Genghis Khan
Timur proclaimed Suyurgatmish and Sultan Mahmud
The monarch: a symbol of national unity
A limited monarchy: crown as symbol

blocks.narration: Explain why Timur, who held real power, put other men on the throne. The answer lies in legitimacy. The title of khan came with the Turks, and dynasties sought legitimacy by tracing their lineage to Genghis Khan for the sake of the title of khan. Timur was not a Chinggisid, so he proclaimed the Chinggisids Suyurgatmish and Sultan Mahmud titular khans. They were puppet rulers: the crown was a symbol of the unity of the nation, while the actual government belonged to Timur. The tests ask exactly this: the practice of appointing a khan with limited power was followed by Amir Timur himself; Suyurgatmish and Sultan Mahmud were puppet rulers.

blocks.heading: Why Did Strong States Fall?
blocks.problem: What factors led to the crisis of large and strong countries?

steps.text: Political instability and internal wars
The struggle for the throne
The disloyalty of the officials
External forces made the weakened state their prey
The people lost trust in the dynasty

blocks.narration: The lecture asks: what factors led to the crisis of large and strong countries? Political instability, internal wars and the struggle for the throne, and the disloyalty of personnel, the officials. These factors weakened states, making them easy prey for external forces. And the people lost trust in and loyalty to rulers and dynasties because of the instability. The lesson of the lecture is that the drawbacks of political instability are equally ruinous for ancient states and for modern ones. When asked this in the exam, name the three causes, instability and internal wars, the disloyal officials, and the loss of the people's trust, and close with the lesson: instability ruins states of every epoch.

Chapter three in brief. Statehood here is about three thousand years old, a monarchy until nineteen twenty. Learn the six periods of ancient statehood, and the four primary states: Bactria, Sogd, Khorezm and Dayuan. The Samanids governed through the dargah and ten diwans. Timur took power in thirteen seventy and ruled through titular khans. Remember: political instability, disloyal officials and lost trust ruined the strongest states.

blocks.title: 1924: Delimitation and Borders
blocks.subtitle: How the map of Central Asia was redrawn
blocks.narration: Chapter four. Nineteen twenty-four: the map of Central Asia is redrawn. The Soviet state creates five national republics by language, the pan-Turkic dream of the Jadids is shattered, and the new borders become a problem that is still being solved today. Nation-building, delimitation, demarcation: the vocabulary of this chapter.

blocks.heading: The Soviet Republic is Born
bullets: March 1927: constitution of the Uzbek SSR
Uzbeks in the apparatus: 23 to 32.3 percent
blocks.narration: The constitution of nineteen twenty-four proclaimed the voluntary principle of the federal structure of the USSR. The constitution of the Uzbek SSR, adopted in March nineteen twenty-seven, declared the republic an equal-in-rights and sovereign component of the USSR, on paper. The government was headed by Fayzulla Khodjayev, who advanced the interests of the local population: the share of Uzbeks in the central organs grew from twenty-three to thirty-two point three percent between nineteen twenty-four and twenty-eight, and reached seventy-five percent in the lower apparatus by the end of nineteen thirty. Yet the USSR methodically intensified hyper-centralisation.

blocks.heading: Nation-Building by Language
bullets: name the population a single people
blocks.narration: In the nineteen twenties came the era of purposeful nation-building. The Soviet state created five republics in stages: the Kazakh, Kirghiz, Uzbek, Tajik and Turkmen ones. The pan-Turkic dream of the Jadids, a single Turanian state with a single language, was shattered into five national states, of which four are Turkic-speaking and one, Tajikistan, is Persian-speaking. The principles of language nationalism were applied: define a territory by language and the supposed common history, name the population a single people, and give it a single state. This is the national-territorial delimitation of nineteen twenty-four. The goal was homo sovieticus, a person who thinks, behaves and lives in the Soviet way.

blocks.heading: Exceptions to the Principles
blocks.narration: The principles had exceptions, and the tests love them. Kazakhstan consisted of Kazakhs and Russians in roughly equal shares, and both were minorities: this is the titular nationality, the people who give the republic its name. In Uzbekistan the Karakalpak Autonomous Republic was set apart for a different language; in Tajikistan, Badakhshan. The Soviet system promoted the Turkic languages and Tajik into modern languages and ensured universal literacy, accompanied by korenizatsiya, the preferment of local cadres. The new nations were built from above and from below, but without sovereignty; the party leaders became the national leaders, which in nineteen ninety-one turned the republics into nation-states.

blocks.heading: The Four Border Terms
blocks.narration: Border-making has its own vocabulary; know all four terms. A treaty is a general term for all instruments binding under international law between two or more legal persons; the Vienna Convention of nineteen sixty-nine defines it as an international agreement concluded in written form and governed by international law. Delimitation is a legal process in which two sovereign states establish and describe in writing the location of their common border, mostly at the negotiating table. Demarcation is a field operation: marking the border on the ground with physical signs. Delineation is the graphic or mathematical representation of the border; often one commission conducts both demarcation and delineation.

blocks.heading: Uzbekistan's Borders Today
bullets: no inviolable areas in the north
blocks.narration: Negotiations with Kazakhstan cover the longest borders of Uzbekistan; settlements are crossed by the border without inviolable areas in the north of the Tashkent and Syrdarya regions, and the two countries chose different paths: protectionism here, liberalisation there. Negotiations with Kyrgyzstan run through the most densely populated regions, the Tashkent, Namangan, Andijan and Fergana regions; Uzbekistan has three enclaves there, and disputes continue in the water sphere. Solving delimitation brings stable borders, transit and partnership in energy, agriculture and industry, a win-win for every side. Part of the archival materials on the borders is still secret, which slows the research.

blocks.heading: From Delimitation to Nation-States
blocks.narration: Put the chapter on one line. Nineteen twenty-four: the national-territorial delimitation divides Central Asia into five national republics. March nineteen twenty-seven: the constitution of the Uzbek SSR declares the republic sovereign, on paper. Through the nineteen twenties, korenizatsiya advanced local cadres, but by the end of the decade it was curtailed, and a hyper-centralized model took root. The republics lived without sovereignty under the ideological homogenization of the party. Then, in nineteen ninety-one, the party leaders had become national leaders, and the republics turned into nation-states. The borders drawn in nineteen twenty-four are still being negotiated today. That is the irony of this chapter.

blocks.heading: Why Draw Borders by Language?
blocks.problem: Why did the Soviet state delimit Central Asia along linguistic lines?

steps.text: The Jadids dreamed of one Turanian state
The Soviet state chose the opposite
Define a territory by language and history
Name the population a single people
Five republics: four Turkic, one Persian

blocks.narration: Explain the logic of nineteen twenty-four. The Jadids dreamed of a single Turanian state with a single language. The Soviet state chose the opposite, the principles of language nationalism: define a territory by language and the supposed common history; name the population a single people; give that people a single state. The result: the pan-Turkic dream was shattered into five national states, of which four are Turkic-speaking and one, Tajikistan, is Persian-speaking. The nations were built from above, without sovereignty, under the ideological homogenization of the party. And in nineteen ninety-one those republics turned into nation-states: the map of nineteen twenty-four became the political map of a new Central Asia.

Chapter four in brief. In nineteen twenty-four the national-territorial delimitation created five republics on the linguistic principle, without sovereignty. Remember the exceptions: Kazakhstan's titular nationality, Karakalpakstan inside Uzbekistan, Badakhshan inside Tajikistan. Know the four border terms: treaty, delimitation, demarcation, delineation. The republics built without sovereignty became nation-states in nineteen ninety-one, and their borders are still being negotiated today.

chapters.title: The Soviet Period: Repression, War and Resources

blocks.title: The Soviet Period
blocks.subtitle: What it gave, and what it took away
blocks.narration: Chapter five. The Soviet period: what it gave and what it took. Collectivisation and the cotton monoculture, four waves of repression, the war against fascism, and the plundering of resources. This is the chapter with the most numbers; learn them, they appear directly in the tests.

blocks.heading: Collectivisation and the Cotton Monoculture
blocks.narration: Collectivisation was carried out forcibly: dehkans were driven into kolkhozes under the threat of deprivation of land, water and food; resisters were dekulakized, their property confiscated and they deported. Between nineteen thirty and thirty-three, forty thousand dehkan households were dekulakized and thirty-one thousand seven hundred dehkans repressed; the ruin of agriculture caused a famine that ended only in nineteen thirty-five. In parallel, the cotton monoculture grew: in nineteen thirty-three cotton accounted for eighty-one and a half percent of agricultural produce, and by nineteen thirty-seven, ninety-three point four percent. In nineteen forty Uzbekistan supplied sixty-three percent of the all-union cotton.

blocks.heading: The Four Phases of Repression
blocks.narration: Phase one, the nineteen twenties to the early thirties: the rollback from the New Economic Policy; the victims were the national intelligentsia and alternative politicians, the underground Milliy Istiqlol of Munavvar Qari. Phase two, nineteen thirty-six to thirty-nine, the Great Terror: the fabricated cases of Khodjayev and Ikramov; by the spring of nineteen thirty-eight more than seventy percent of the leaders had been repressed, the NKVD troikas imprisoned forty-one thousand, six thousand nine hundred twenty shot; the intelligentsia, Qodiriy, Chulpon and Fitrat, was destroyed. Phase three, nineteen forty-six to fifty-three, struck financiers and war veterans. Phase four, nineteen eighty-three to eighty-five, the Cotton Affair: Gdlyan and Ivanov, more than twenty-five thousand arrested.

blocks.heading: Literacy and Deculturation
bullets: prison terms for the Arabic script
blocks.narration: Literacy grew from about eleven percent in nineteen twenty-eight to sixty-eight percent in nineteen thirty-nine. By nineteen forty the republic had five thousand five hundred four schools and almost one million four hundred thousand pupils, against eighty-two thousand in nineteen twenty-four. But the negative side was heavy: the change of alphabets brought a new wave of illiteracy, and prison terms of ten to fifteen years were given for publication in the Arabic script. In nineteen thirty-eight Russian became compulsory in national schools; in nineteen forty the Cyrillic script was introduced by decree. Culture was to be socialist in content, internationalist in spirit, national in form.

blocks.heading: Deportations and the War
blocks.narration: The first deported were the Far East Koreans: between September and December nineteen thirty-seven, more than seventy-four thousand five hundred arrived in Uzbekistan. In nineteen forty-three and forty-four came the exiles: about one hundred ten thousand Meskhetian Turks and one hundred fifty-one thousand four hundred twenty-four Crimean Tatars. Then the war. One million four hundred thirty-three thousand two hundred thirty took part, over forty percent of the able-bodied population; two hundred sixty-three thousand five killed, one hundred thirty-two thousand six hundred seventy missing, three hundred ninety-five thousand seven hundred ninety-five who did not return, sixty thousand four hundred fifty-two invalids. Two hundred eighty became Heroes of the Soviet Union, seventy-five Uzbeks. More than one hundred enterprises and more than one million evacuees, including two hundred thousand children, were received, many adopted by Uzbek families.

blocks.heading: A Raw-Material Appendage
blocks.narration: After Stalin, the republic grew: under Sharaf Rashidov, by nineteen eighty-five one thousand five hundred forty-nine were functioning, with one hundred ninety-seven thousand kilometers of canals and twenty-three reservoirs. But the losses were enormous. In the nineteen eighties annual gas deliveries exceeded two hundred fifty billion cubic metres, gold more than fifty tonnes; minerals, about five and a half billion dollars a year. In the last fifteen years of the USSR, cotton and gold worth no less than thirty-five billion were taken away, minerals more than seventy-five billion. The cotton monoculture and the uncontrolled use of the two rivers led to the tragedy of the Aral Sea.

blocks.heading: Why the Great Terror?
blocks.problem: Why did the system strike first at the intelligentsia?

steps.text: Repression built homo sovieticus
Reprisals 'watered' the Soviet ideology
The troikas: 41,000 imprisoned, 6,920 shot
Qodiriy, Chulpon, Fitrat destroyed
Fear kept the rest obedient

blocks.result: Fear as an instrument of control
blocks.narration: Why did the Soviet Union pursue a harsh repressive policy? Because repression was an instrument of building homo sovieticus and of suppressing any resistance. Physical reprisal against the intelligentsia and influential people facilitated the watering of Soviet ideology; intimidation maintained the loyalty of the poor, from whom the property of the rich was nationalized. The first professor of history, Pulat Saliev, was killed; the writers Qodiriy, Chulpon and Fitrat, destroyed. The NKVD troikas, tribunals of three, imprisoned more than forty-one thousand, six thousand nine hundred twenty of them shot. In nineteen thirty-seven to fifty-three, almost one hundred thousand were repressed, thirteen thousand shot. The four phases sowed fear and destroyed the national elites.

Chapter five in brief. Forced collectivisation dekulakized forty thousand households and caused a famine that ended only in nineteen thirty-five. Repression came in four phases, from the rollback of the NEP to the Cotton Affair. Literacy grew from eleven to sixty-eight percent, but at the price of deculturation. One million four hundred thousand fought in the war; two hundred eighty became Heroes of the Soviet Union. And the republic's resources, cotton, gold and gas, were taken for the needs of the centre.

blocks.title: The Road to Independence
blocks.subtitle: Perestroika, 1990, 1991
blocks.narration: Chapter six, the final chapter: perestroika and the road to independence. From Gorbachev's reforms of nineteen eighty-five through the Declaration of nineteen ninety to the proclamation of independence on the thirty-first of August, nineteen ninety-one, and the referendum that confirmed it in December.

blocks.heading: Perestroika and the Demonstrations of 1989
blocks.narration: Perestroika was proclaimed by Mikhail Gorbachev in April nineteen eighty-five, the hope of an exit from the systemic crisis, with a new thinking in foreign policy for the sake of universal human values. Glasnost weakened the ideological yoke, and national movements were born with demands for democratic reform and genuine sovereignty, for the rebirth of national consciousness and the restoration of statehood. The wave of demonstrations of nineteen eighty-nine swept through Fergana, Kokand, Kuvasay, Gulistan, Parkent and Buka. In the same year the Uzbek language was given the status of the state language, and measures began to liquidate the cotton monoculture and restore spirituality.

blocks.heading: 1990: President and Declaration
bullets: the first among the union republics
blocks.narration: In March nineteen ninety, Islam Karimov was elected president at the first session of the twelfth convocation of the Supreme Soviet of the Uzbek SSR, an unprecedented step: not a single union region had elected a president before, and the centre reacted extremely negatively. Political sovereignty and economic self-reliance were advanced as its decisive conditions. The Declaration of Independence was adopted at the second session on the eighteenth to twentieth of June, nineteen ninety: twelve articles enshrining the supremacy of the democratic state and of the laws, the independent resolution of internal and foreign policy, and one's own path of development.

blocks.heading: 1991: The Year of Independence
blocks.narration: Nineteen ninety-one. On the nineteenth of August came the last attempt to preserve the USSR: an unconstitutional coup, the State Committee for the State of Emergency, the GKChP; Gorbachev was isolated; Karimov's India visit was interrupted. The sixth session adopted the Statement on independence and the Law on the Foundations of State Independence. On the thirty-first of August, independence was proclaimed; the first of September became Independence Day, a day off since nineteen ninety-one. And on the twenty-ninth of December, the referendum confirmed the people's support, more than ninety-eight percent. The same day, the first presidential election made Karimov the first President.

blocks.heading: Why 31 August?
blocks.problem: How did the August coup accelerate independence?

steps.text: 19 August 1991: the GKChP coup in Moscow
Gorbachev isolated; India visit interrupted
The sixth session adopts Statement and Law
31 August: independence proclaimed
1 September declared Independence Day

blocks.narration: Explain why independence came at the end of August nineteen ninety-one. The trigger was the coup. On the nineteenth of August, the State Committee for the State of Emergency tried to preserve the USSR by unconstitutional force. Gorbachev was isolated; Karimov's visit to India was interrupted. The attempt failed, and the emergency sixth session adopted the Statement on the independence of Uzbekistan and the Law on the Foundations of State Independence. On the thirty-first of August, independence was proclaimed; the first of September was declared Independence Day and a day off, beginning with nineteen ninety-one. The union collapsed, and the republic took its sovereignty without waiting for the centre's permission.

blocks.heading: The Attributes of Sovereignty
bullets: a president: 35 years, state language, 10 years
blocks.narration: Independence needs attributes. The Constitutional Law on the Foundations of State Independence was adopted on the thirty-first of August, nineteen ninety-one. On the twenty-ninth of December, the referendum: more than ninety-eight percent supported independence, and on the same day the first nationwide elections of the President were held, universal, equal and direct. A candidate must be a citizen not younger than thirty-five years, must command the state language and have lived in Uzbekistan for at least ten years. The emblem, the flag, the anthem and the national currency became the attributes of sovereignty.

blocks.heading: The Historical Significance of Independence
blocks.problem: What does independence mean for a state with three thousand years of history?

steps.text: Restoration of a 3000-year statehood
One's own constitutional path; market reforms
Revival of national values and spirituality
Equal membership in the world community
From dependent republic to nation-state

blocks.narration: Close the course with the meaning of it all. The historical significance of independence consists of the restoration of the sovereign statehood of a three-thousand-year tradition. Remember the arc of this video: from Northern Bactria through the Samanids and Timur to the khanates; then dependence, delimitation and the Soviet period; and now, at last, sovereignty. Independence gave Uzbekistan its own constitutional path and market reforms, the Uzbek model with its five principles; the revival of national values and spirituality, the return of historical memory; and equal membership in the world community. A dependent republic became a nation-state, master of its own resources, its own language and its own future.

Chapter six in brief. April nineteen eighty-five: perestroika. Nineteen eighty-nine: the state language, and demonstrations across the region. March nineteen ninety: Karimov becomes the first president. June nineteen ninety: the Declaration of Independence, twelve articles. The thirty-first of August, nineteen ninety-one: independence proclaimed; the first of September becomes Independence Day. And on the twenty-ninth of December, the referendum confirmed it, and the first President was elected.

items: history: experience first — then thought, fact
civilization: Jeitun to the Bronze Age
blocks.narration: The whole course in one view. History is an inquiry into the past on the basis of evidence, where experience matters most. Central Asia is one of the centers of world civilization: Jeitun's first agriculture, Kelteminar's fishers, the proto-cities of the Bronze Age. Statehood runs about three thousand years: Bactria, Sogd, Khorezm and Dayuan; the Samanids with their dargah and ten diwans; Timur and the Timurids; the three khanates. Nineteen twenty-four drew the map of five republics by language. The Soviet period brought repression, war and the loss of resources, and also literacy and industry. And nineteen ninety-one restored sovereignty. Learn the cheat sheet of dates and numbers.
